phonemes.desc: Short alpha with smooth breathing — the name opens clearly, without roughness.
Aspirated theta [tʰ], the sound of intellect: precise, sharp, clean.
Long eta with acute pitch — the stressed peak of the name, holding authority.
Long alpha with iota subscript, the old nominative ending that gives the name its archaic dignity.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ah-THAY-na' — the second syllable is pitched higher and drawn out; the final 'a' is long and pure.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: Ἀθήνη (Athḗnē), the older form; the long final alpha reflects the original stem

kin.label: Luwian
kin.form: Attarsiya, a theophoric name in Bronze Age Anatolia, possibly related

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: no secure etymology; Beekes treats the name as Pre-Greek

pronunciation.note: Athénā is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἀθήνᾶ contains both stress (acute on the long η) and length (η plus long alpha with iota subscript). The restoration Athénā preserves the acute stress; Athēnā is the macron-only variant. The form Athēnē changes the final letter and is therefore used only when the domain requires it.

domains.title: The Grey-Eyed Strategist
domains.subtitle: Wisdom, Warcraft, Crafts, and Civilization
domains.lead: Athénā is unique among the Olympians: a warrior who fights only for just causes, a virgin goddess who needs no consort to validate her power, and the patron of the practical arts that make city life possible. She is intelligence made divine.

cards.name: Strategic Warfare
cards.desc: She favors counsel, discipline, and defensive battle over the berserk fury of Árēs; heroes like Odysseus and Diomedes fight under her sign.

cards.name: Wisdom and Counsel
cards.desc: The mind that sees all sides; her advice is practical, ethical, and far-sighted.

cards.name: Weaving and Crafts
cards.desc: Patron of weaving, pottery, carpentry, and olive cultivation — the technologies that sustain the polis.

cards.name: Guardian of Cities
cards.desc: Polias and Poliouchos: the goddess who protects the citadel and whose olive tree marks the land.

symbols.name: Owl

symbols.name: Olive tree
symbols.meaning: Her gift to Athens, defeat of Poseidôn in the contest for the city

symbols.name: Aegis
symbols.meaning: The goat-skin fringed with serpents; worn by Zeús and Athena, it inspires terror

symbols.name: Helmet and spear
symbols.meaning: Warrior identity, but always disciplined and defensive

symbols.name: Gorgoneion
symbols.meaning: The severed head of Medousa on her breastplate, turning enemies to stone

symbols.name: Spindle and loom
symbols.meaning: Weaving as the emblem of ordered, intelligent labor

mythology.lead: Athénā's myths center on intelligence overcoming force. She is born from Zeús's head, defeats Poseidôn by gift rather than combat, and guides the heroes who win by cunning.

myths.title: Born from the Head of Zeús
myths.text: Zeús swallowed his pregnant first wife Mêtis, fearing a son who would overthrow him. Later, Hephaistos split Zeús's skull with an axe, and Athénā sprang forth fully armed with a shout that shook Olympus. She is therefore the only Olympian whose parent is purely paternal — intelligence born directly from sovereignty.

myths.title: Athena and Poseidôn for Athens
myths.text: The two gods competed to become patron of Athens. Poseidôn struck the Acropolis with his trident and produced a salt spring; Athénā planted the first olive tree. The judges — Cecrops and the Athenian people — chose the olive, because it gives food, oil, and wood. Poseidôn flooded the land in anger, but Athénā's city endured. The myth makes civilization superior to maritime power.

myths.title: Arachnê Transformed
myths.text: The mortal weaver Arachnê boasted that her skill surpassed the goddess's. Athénā wove a tapestry of the gods' glory; Arachnê wove their scandals. Though flawless, Arachnê's work was impious. Athénā struck her, and in remorse or punishment the maiden hanged herself. The goddess transformed her into the first spider. The myth is a warning: skill without reverence is hubris.

myths.title: Odysseus and the Return
myths.text: Athénā's favorite mortal is Odysseus, the man of many wiles. She protects him through his wanderings, disguises him on Ithaca, and stands with him against the suitors. Their bond is the closest thing in Greek myth to a partnership between human intelligence and divine wisdom.

lore.syncretism: The Romans identified Athénā with Minerva, a goddess already associated with crafts and strategy, so the equation was unusually smooth. In Egypt she was equated with Neith, the warrior-weaver goddess of Sais, and Hellenistic Jews identified her with Sophia, divine Wisdom. During the Renaissance she became the emblem of rational virtue; in modern Athens she remains the namesake and symbol of the city, her helmeted head on coins and official seals. The Parthenon, her temple, is the canonical image of Classical Greece.
lore.culturalLegacy: Athénā is the divine patron of everything the Greeks most valued in civic life: wisdom, craft, disciplined courage, and strategic thought. The Athenian democracy claimed her protection; the Panathenaea was the city's greatest festival. In philosophy she became the emblem of reason; in art the model of dignified female power. Her owl, her olive, and her helmet are still instantly recognizable symbols of classical civilization. Restoring Athénā preserves the name under which the world's first democracy invoked its guiding intelligence.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Athénā is the goddess of the well-aimed blow — not merely in war, but in speech, craft, and thought. She does not rage; she calculates. She does not seduce; she advises. Her virginity is not a lack but a statement: her power is complete in itself, needing no alliance with masculinity to be effective.

In an age that often confuses intelligence with cleverness and power with dominance, Athénā offers a different model. She is strong because she is skilled, just because she is wise, and feared because she is right. The restoration of her name in Unicode is a small act of recognition: that wisdom, no less than beauty or wrath, deserves its original voice.
lore.archaeology: The Athenian Acropolis preserves the Parthenon (447–432 BCE), Erechtheion, and Temple of Athena Nike, whose sculptural program celebrated Athena Polias, Parthenos, and Nikephoros. The colossal gold-and-ivory Athena Parthenos by Pheidias stood inside the Parthenon; fragments of its base survive. The Panathenaic frieze and pedimental sculptures show the goddess in birth and triumph. Outside Athens, the temple of Athena Alea at Tegea and the sanctuary at Lindos on Rhodes attest her wide civic cult.
